title: Advancing Education through Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad question of how tutoring systems have evolved and what educational value they currently provide, with a focus on intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) and robot tutoring systems (RTS). It asks how these systems developed from early computer-assisted instruction into modern AI-driven tools, how they adapt to student needs in real time, and what ethical issues arise from their use. The review also considers the role of generative AI and large language models in extending tutoring capabilities.

The authors conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 86 representative studies published between 1972 and 2024. Rather than studying one new intervention, the paper synthesizes prior work across computer-based ITS, robot-based RTS, and multimodal hybrid systems. The review framework organizes evidence around artificial intelligence, system behavior, engagement, and affordances, and it uses latent class analysis to classify systems into three groups: computer-based ITS, verbal robot-based tutoring systems, and multimodal systems.

The paper concludes that software-based ITS are strongest in cognitive adaptability, personalized feedback, and scalability, while robot-based systems are especially effective for social and emotional engagement. It finds that generative AI and LLMs are expanding the responsiveness of tutoring systems, but also introduce risks related to hallucination, privacy, fairness, and transparency. The authors argue that future progress depends on hybrid designs that combine the cognitive strengths of ITS with the motivational and relational strengths of RTS, alongside stronger ethical governance and responsible AI practices.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic literature review using PRISMA and latent class analysis, which supports a structured synthesis. However, it is not a primary causal study and does not provide pooled effect estimates or direct experimental evidence for most outcomes, so it falls below meta-analysis/RCT standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper argues for positive educational impact of ITS and robot tutors, especially for engagement and adaptive support, but it does not report effect sizes for the review’s synthesized findings. The evidence is therefore directionally favorable but still unclear/modest in measurable impact terms.

interventions.use_case: Systematic review of AI-driven tutoring systems, especially computer-based ITS using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, concept trees, fuzzy logic, and other adaptive models to personalize instruction and feedback for K-12 and related learners.

Systematic review of robot tutoring systems (RTS) and embodied tutors that use physical presence, gestures, verbal encouragement, and multimodal interaction to support student engagement and learning.
Reviews modern generative AI and LLM-based tutoring uses, including ChatGPT-style tutors, LLM-powered feedback, adaptive language tutoring, and conversational teaching assistants.
Covers early computer-assisted instruction systems as historical predecessors to ITS, including static or minimally adaptive software-delivered tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that software-based ITS and hybrid tutoring systems generally improve math learning outcomes through adaptive difficulty, real-time feedback, and personalized content. Specific examples cited include a middle-school mathematics ITS and a 6th-grade math tutoring system, but the paper is a systematic review and does not report a single pooled effect size for math achievement.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement / learning outcomes in tutoring studies
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed; individual math-study samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that tutoring systems, including LLM-based tutors and robot-assisted systems, can support science learning by delivering personalized explanations and adaptive feedback. It cites physics education and STEM-related tutoring examples, but no aggregated effect size or single study-level estimate is reported in the review text.
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed; individual science-study samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that robot-based tutoring systems enhance motivation, emotional engagement, and social interaction through gestures, verbal praise, and human-like presence. The review repeatedly contrasts this strength with software-based ITS, but it does not provide a pooled effect size; the evidence is synthesized from 86 studies and cites prior meta-analytic and field-trial work.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, attitudes toward learning, social-emotional engagement
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed; individual study samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that ITS and LLM-powered tutors improve engagement by providing immediate, personalized, and conversational feedback that sustains student attention and interest. While the direction is positive, the paper does not report a pooled effect size or standardized estimate for engagement outcomes.
finding.measure: Student engagement, attention, motivation, interaction quality
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed; individual study samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that tutoring systems can support problem-solving and deeper understanding by adapting explanations and prompts to student responses, especially in multimodal and LLM-enabled systems. This is presented as a broad synthesis rather than a quantified effect, so no effect size is available.
finding.measure: Problem-solving, deeper understanding, adaptive reasoning support
finding.study_size: n=86 studies reviewed; individual study samples not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review finds meaningful promise for tutoring systems but also persistent institutional challenges, especially scalability, data privacy, fairness, and ethical governance. It frames these as unresolved system-level issues rather than measured intervention effects, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Ethical concerns, scalability, deployment feasibility, governance considerations
